newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss reject U.S. charge it helped prolong WWII.
newsitem.headline: Swiss reject U.S. charge it helped prolong WWII.

text.p: Switzerland denied on Thursday that its business deals with Nazi Germany prolonged World War Two.
In its first detailed response to a critical U.S. report this month, the Swiss government acknowledged some "questionable deals" with the Axis powers.
But it rejected portrayal of neutral Switzerland as "bankers to the Nazis" and said there was no need to reopen a post-war treaty on the return of looted gold bought from Hitler's Germany.

Taking the offensive, it also defended Swiss neutrality as the best way to preserve the country's independence when surrounded by fascist powers and dismissed suggestions the Swiss were cold blooded profiteers unmoved by the horrors raging around them.

Berne criticised the foreword of the U.S. study, compiled by Under-secretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat and the State Department's chief historian, which it said "contains political and moral judgements which go beyond the historical report".

"It is suggested in the foreword that the neutral countries may have prolonged the Third Reich's ability to wage war by trading with it. This comment must be referred to as unsupported, at least based on the report's contents," it said.

The Eizenstat report's critique of Swiss commerce with the Nazis failed to address adequately Switzerland's battle for political and economic survival and its trade with the Allies, the government said, although Swiss business benefited as well.

"There were at the same time questionable deals as well which did not affect the survival of Switzerland," it said, but added it was hard to say whether Switzerland could have broken off commerce in 1943 or 1944 without provoking an Axis invasion.

"The Federal Council (cabinet) regards the representation of Switzerland as the banker to the Nazis as a one-sided broad-brush judgement," it said, again citing its ties with the Allies and its long history of links to pre-Nazi Germany.

The government also rejected U.S. criticism of Switzerland's hard line in talks after World War Two about returning gold it bought from Germany, much of which the Nazis had looted from occupied countries, some even from the teeth of Holocaust victims.

Switzerland agreed with the Allies in 1946 to pay 250 million Swiss francs in gold (then worth 58 million dollars) as a voluntary contribution to European reconstruction in return for the Allies dropping all claims related to the gold deals.

"At the conclusion of the Washington Agreement in 1946 the parties to the signing realised all the essential facts. Thanks to their intelligence sources, the Allies even had precise knowledge of the Swiss negotiating position," the cabinet said.

Allied demands that Switzerland hand over German assets without compensation flew in the face of the rule of law, it said, but added historians would have to judge whether the Swiss had taken too narrow a legalistic approach in the talks.

Stung by charges the Swiss cynically profited from the war, the cabinet said neutrality was the only way Switzerland could be maintained as a haven for tens of thousands of refugees and "an oasis of democracy and freedom in a totalitarian Europe".
"The Swiss people have never understood neutrality as mere indifference in convictions," it said.
Vowing to work together with its critics to find the truth about its wartime past, Switzerland acknowledged some errors.

"All in all, neutrality led to a difficult tightrope walk between adaptation and resistance. Today we know that this also led to mistakes. The faint-hearted refugee policy for Jews was inexcusable," it said.
It was referring to Berne's anti-Jewish policy that turned back tens of thousands of refugees as the Holocaust raged and forced Jewish groups to pay for the upkeep of Jews allowed in.

The government highlighted steps taken recently to shed light on the past. The government has relaxed bank secrecy for two independent panels, one hunting dormant bank accounts of Holocaust victims and another writing a broad history of the Swiss role as a financial centre during World War Two.

It has also set up a memorial fund with 265 million Swiss francs in donations from banks and businesses to aid needy Holocaust victims and their families, and has proposed selling off gold reserves to fund humanitarian aid to victims of poverty and disasters in Switzerland and abroad.
